positions.as_written: Measure strain, force or motion in a living knee.
Measure a shape or a position from a scan and relate it to an event.
Follow patients and record what happened.
Read the design before the abstract, since the design bounds every claim the abstract makes.
Ask what the comparator was, and treat its absence as a reason to downgrade rather than as a detail.
Read chapter 3.17 by subject when a specific study matters, and read this page's five designs when a new paper arrives in a subject you do not know.
The decision this page informs is how much weight a landmark study should carry when a patient is in front of you, and the answer is a balance rather than a rule.
Consider their age and physiology, because a finding from elderly specimens transfers differently to a young knee.
Consider their comorbidities, which change healing and rehabilitation in ways no cadaveric study measures.
Consider the demands on their knee, since that determines which of the mechanical findings is relevant and which is academic.
Consider their psychological state, because confidence and fear of reinjury predict function more strongly than laxity does.
Record which way the balance fell and what evidence you weighted, since that is what makes the decision reviewable later.
